     A_T) \mathrm{d} \lambda = \int^{\infty}_0 \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\lambda} (A_T, A_T) \mathrm{d}
     \lambda + \frac{1}{4 \pi} \| A_T \|^2_{L^2} . \]
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Write $\Pi^{\lambda,M}(0)=c_M(\lambda)I_2$ and
  $\Pi^\lambda(0)=c(\lambda)I_2$.
  Since $A_T$ is smooth, it is sufficient to show the following things:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \par\hangindent 40\p@\label{item:Gal-symbol} $\Pi^{\lambda, M} (p) - \Pi^{\lambda, M} (0) \rightarrow
    \Pi^{\lambda} (p) - \Pi^{\lambda} (0)$ $\forall p \neq 0$ , and $\|
    \Pi^{\lambda, M} (p) - \Pi^{\lambda, M} (0) \| \leqslant | p |^2 (1 +
    \lambda)^{- 2}$.

    \par\hangindent 40\p@\label{item:Gal-zero-mode} $\int c_M(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda - \int c(\lambda)
    \mathrm{d} \lambda \rightarrow \frac{1}{4 \pi}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the statement will follow since, applying Fourier isometry, we get

  \begin{align}
     \int^{\infty}_0 \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\lambda , M} (A_T, A_T) \mathrm{d} \lambda
    = & \int^{\infty}_0 \sum_{p \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \hat{A}_T(p)^* \Pi^{\lambda, M} (p)
    \hat{A}_T(p) \mathrm{d} \lambda \nonumber\\
    = & \int^{\infty}_0 \sum_{p \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \hat{A}_T(p)^* (\Pi^{\lambda, M} (p)
    - \Pi^{\lambda, M} (0)) \hat{A}_T(p) \mathrm{d}\lambda \nonumber\\
    &\quad + \| A_T \|^2_{L^2} \int^{\infty}_0 c_M(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda . \nonumber
  \end{align}

  By~(\ref{item:Gal-symbol}), dominated convergence applies to the
  first term, and~(\ref{item:Gal-zero-mode}) then gives the result.
  For~(\ref{item:Gal-symbol}), repeat the estimates in the proof of
  Lemma~\ref{lem:vac_pol_bound} for each matrix entry. The terms
  odd in $q$ still cancel under the restriction $|q|\le M$.
  For~(\ref{item:Gal-zero-mode}), the definition of $c_M(\lambda)$ gives

  \begin{align}
    \int c_M(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda & = \int^{\infty}_0
    \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2, | q | \leqslant M} \frac{(1 + \lambda - |
    q |^2)}{(1 + \lambda + | q |^2)^3} \mathrm{d}\lambda \nonumber\\
    & = - \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2, | q | \leqslant M}
    \int^{\infty}_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\lambda} \frac{(1 + \lambda)}{(1 +
    \lambda + | q |^2)^2} \mathrm{d} \lambda \nonumber\\
    & = \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2, | q | \leqslant M}
    \frac{1}{(1 + | q |^2)^2} . \nonumber
  \end{align}

  To compare this with $\int^{\infty}_0 c(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda$, we
  fist recall that that $c(\lambda)$ is integrable in $\lambda$, so
  $\int^{\infty}_0 c(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda = \lim_{L \rightarrow
  \infty} \int^L_0 c(\lambda) \mathrm{d} \lambda$. Then recalling that the
  sum which defined $c(\lambda)$ converges absolutely (for fixed $\lambda
  !$), we obtain by Fubini
  \begin{align}
    \int^{\infty}_0 c(\lambda) \,\mathrm{d} \lambda & = \lim_{L \rightarrow
    \infty} \int^L_0 \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{(1 + \lambda - | q
    |^2)}{(1 + \lambda + | q |^2)^3} \,\mathrm{d} \lambda \nonumber\\
    & = \lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \int^L_0
    \frac{(1 + \lambda - | q |^2)}{(1 + \lambda + | q |^2)^3} \,\mathrm{d} \lambda
    \nonumber\\
    & = \lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} - \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2}
    \int^L_0 \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d} \lambda} \frac{(1 + \lambda)}{(1 + \lambda +
    | q |^2)^2} \,\mathrm{d} \lambda \nonumber\\
    & = \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{1}{(1 + | q |^2)^2} - \lim_{L
    \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{1 + L}{(1 + L +
    | q |^2)^2} . \nonumber
  \end{align}
  Dominated convergence easily shows that $\sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2, | q
  | \leqslant M} \frac{1}{(1 + | q |^2)^2} - \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2,}
  \frac{1}{(1 + | q |^2)^2}$ tends to $0$ as $M \rightarrow \infty$. It thus
  remains to show that the last term equals $\frac{1}{4 \pi}$. Indeed

  \begin{align}
    & \lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{q \in 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{1 +
    L}{(1 + L + | q |^2)^2} \nonumber\\
    = & \lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} (1 + L)^{- 1} \sum_{q \in 2 \pi
    \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{1}{\left( 1 + \frac{| q |^2}{1 + L} \right)^2} .
    \nonumber
  \end{align}
  Now relabelling $\sqrt{1 + L}^{- 1} q = \tilde{q}$, this becomes

  \begin{align}
    \lim_{L \rightarrow \infty} (1 + L)^{- 1} \sum_{\tilde{q} \in \frac{2
    \pi}{\sqrt{1 + L}} \mathbb{Z}^2} \frac{1}{(1 + | \tilde{q} |^2)^2} & =
    \frac{1}{4 \pi^2} \int \frac{1}{(1 + | x |^2)^2} \,\mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{4
    \pi}, \nonumber
  \end{align}
  where the first equality follows by Riemann sum approximation. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:coulomb_representative}
For every $(\bar A,\psi)\in\Omega^1H^1\times H^1(\mathbb{T}^2;{\mathbb C})$, there exists $g\in H^2(\mathbb{T}^2;U(1))$ such that
\[
(A,\phi):=g{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}(\bar A,\psi)\in\Omega^1H^1\times H^1(\mathbb{T}^2;{\mathbb C}),
\qquad
\mathrm{d}^*A=0,\qquad \int_{\mathbb{T}^2}A\,\,\mathrm{d} x\in{\mathbf i}(0,2\pi]^2.
\]
The gauge field $A$ is unique within the gauge orbit.
The transformation $g$ is unique up to a constant in $U(1)$, which acts on $\phi$ by a constant phase rotation.
Moreover,
\[
\mathrm{d} A=\mathrm{d}\bar A,\qquad
\mathrm{d}_A\phi=g\,\mathrm{d}_{\bar A}\psi,\qquad
|\phi|=|\psi|,
\]
so the Yang--Mills--Higgs action is unchanged.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
The Hodge decomposition splits $\bar A$ into orthogonal exact, co-exact and harmonic parts:
\[
\bar A=\mathrm{d}\alpha+\mathrm{d}^*\beta+\gamma,
\]
where $\alpha\in H^2(\mathbb{T}^2;{\mathbf i}\mathbb{R})$ has zero mean, $\beta$ is an $H^2$ $2$-form, and $\gamma=\int_{\mathbb{T}^2}\bar A\,\,\mathrm{d} x$ is constant.
Choose $k\in{\mathbb Z}^2$ such that $\vartheta:=\gamma-2\pi{\mathbf i} k\in{\mathbf i}(0,2\pi]^2$, and set
\[
g_k(x):=e^{2\pi{\mathbf i} k\cdot x},\qquad
g:=e^\alpha g_k,\qquad
A=\mathrm{d}^*\beta+\vartheta.
\]
Then $\mathrm{d} g\,g^{-1}=\mathrm{d}\alpha+2\pi{\mathbf i} k$, so $A=\bar A^g$ satisfies \eqref{eq:Coulomb}.
Sobolev product and composition estimates give $g\in H^2$ and $g\psi\in H^1$, and the product rule gives the stated identities and invariance of the action.

For uniqueness, write any $H^2$ transformation between two such representatives as $h=e^\eta g_\ell$, with $\eta\in H^2(\mathbb{T}^2;{\mathbf i}\mathbb{R})$ and $\ell\in{\mathbb Z}^2$.
The Coulomb condition gives $\mathrm{d}^*\mathrm{d}\eta=0$, so $\eta$ is constant.
Since both harmonic components belong to ${\mathbf i}(0,2\pi]^2$, $\ell=0$ and $h$ is constant.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
